Keywords: The, Kilcloher, God

outputs.L1:
The body of the boy who took his flight
off the cliff at Kilcloher into the sea
was hauled up by the curragh-men, who rowed
at first light, fishing mackerel in the estuary.
"No requiem nor rosary," declared the priest,
"nor consecrated ground for burial,"
as if the boy had flown beyond the pale
of mercy or redemption or God's love.

"Forgive them, for they know not what they do,"
so Argyle intoned above the corpse's kin,
who heard within his words a kind of riddle,
as if he meant their fellow congregants
and not their sodden, sadly broken boy.
Either way, they drew some comfort from it,
and laid out finer fare than was their custom—
of food and spirits; for by their own reckoning,
the greater sin demanded the greater toll.

But Argyle refused their offered shilling
and helped them build a box and dig a grave.
"Your boy's no profligate, nor prodigal,"
he said, "but only a wounded pilgrim, like us all.
What if his leaping was a leap of faith,
into his father's beckoning embrace?"
They killed no fatted calf. They filled the hole.
outputs.L2:
At dawn, fishermen out in their curraghs catching mackerel in the estuary recovered the body of the young man who had leapt from the Kilcloher cliff down into the ocean.

The priest declared there would be "no mass, no prayers said on beads, and no blessed earth in which to lay him," treating the boy as though his fall had carried him beyond the boundaries of God's love, of forgiveness, of any chance at salvation.

Then Argyle spoke to the grieving family: "Forgive them, for they know not what they do." They puzzled over his words as though they held some hidden meaning, wondering if perhaps he was speaking not of the boy but of the priest and his fellow believers—rather than referring to their waterlogged, tragically shattered son.

Whatever he intended, his words brought them a measure of solace, and they laid out finer food and drink than they normally would, following their belief that a heavier sin demands a heavier price.

Yet Argyle would take none of their offered payment. Instead, he lent his hands to fashioning a coffin and digging out the grave.

"Your son was no wastrel, no reckless spendthrift," he told them. "He was simply a hurt traveler, no different from any of us. Who's to say his jump wasn't an act of faith—a plunge straight into the waiting arms of his father?"

No feast was held to celebrate a return. They simply covered over the grave.
outputs.L3:
The boy's body was recovered from the sea by curragh fishermen, who rowed out through the grey swell to gather what the water had given back. He had leaped to his death from the cliff at Kilcloher, and it was there, at the foot of that great wall of stone, that they found him.

The priest denied the boy a religious funeral. He refused him a requiem, refused the rosary, refused burial in consecrated ground—as though the act of suicide had placed the boy forever beyond the reach of God's mercy, cast out from the fold and the forgiveness the Church claimed to hold in trust.

It was Argyle who spoke words of forgiveness over the body. He stood above the boy and pronounced a blessing, though the meaning of it was uncertain to those who listened. The boy's people took his words in two ways at once: some heard in them a quiet rebuke of the priest and his hard judgment, while others heard only comfort meant for themselves, a balm laid gently upon their grief. Argyle left the ambiguity unresolved, and perhaps that was his intention.

When the family offered him payment, Argyle refused it. Instead, he rolled up his sleeves and worked alongside them—helping to build the coffin plank by plank, and to dig the grave with his own hands. He treated the dead boy not as a thing to be hurried into the ground and forgotten, but with dignity, as one worthy of care and of ceremony.

And in the end, Argyle reframed the boy entirely. He was not a sinner to be condemned, Argyle suggested, but a wounded pilgrim who had lost his way in sorrow. His fatal leap from the cliff need not be seen as an act of despair or damnation. It might instead be understood as a leap of faith—a final, desperate flight into the waiting embrace of his father.
outputs.L4:
# A Community's Grief and the Voice of Argyle

The poem unfolds in the aftermath of a devastating loss: a young boy has thrown himself from a cliff, ending his own life. In the tight-knit community left behind, the tragedy reverberates not only as private sorrow but as a public crisis of meaning. The mourners gather, uncertain of how to comprehend an act that seems to defy both reason and consolation. Their grief is raw, and it is made heavier still by the weight of religious judgment that descends upon them.

Into this atmosphere of anguish steps the figure of the priest, who represents the rigid application of doctrine. According to the strictures he upholds, a suicide cannot be granted the sacred burial rites reserved for the faithful. In the eyes of the church he serves, the boy's final act places him outside the boundaries of grace—an offense against the divine order that must be met with denial rather than mercy. For the grieving family and community, this refusal compounds their pain, transforming their loss into a source of shame and their sorrow into something that must be hidden or condemned.

It is here that the character of Argyle emerges as the poem's moral and emotional center. Rather than accepting the priest's cold verdict, Argyle offers a radically different interpretation of the boy's death—one rooted in compassion rather than condemnation. He reframes the tragedy entirely, casting the boy not as a sinner but as "a wounded pilgrim," a soul burdened and injured, yet still journeying toward something greater than himself. In this vision, the boy's suffering is not evidence of his fall from grace but of his humanity and his pain.

Most strikingly, Argyle transforms the fatal plunge itself. What the priest sees as a rejection of God, Argyle redefines as a "leap of faith"—an act of desperate trust rather than despairing rejection. Through this reinterpretation, the boy's final gesture becomes something that can be mourned with tenderness rather than disavowed with horror. Argyle gives the mourners permission to love the boy still, to grieve him openly, and to imagine him embraced rather than cast out.

In offering this consolation, Argyle provides the community with a solace that doctrine alone could never supply. The poem thus dramatizes a profound tension: on one side stands the inflexible authority of religious law, which measures the dead against fixed standards and finds them wanting; on the other stands human mercy, which meets tragedy with understanding and refuses to abandon the suffering. Through Argyle's compassionate voice, the poem ultimately affirms that in the face of unbearable loss, it is mercy—not rigid judgment—that offers the truest form of grace.

# The Kilcloher Blessing

Nestled along the rugged coastline of Ireland, the small townland of Kilcloher carries a quiet reverence that seems woven into its very landscape. Here, where the wind sweeps across ancient fields and the Atlantic hums against the cliffs, the presence of something greater feels close at hand.

The people of Kilcloher have long held a deep connection to their faith. For generations, families gathered to give thanks to God for the harvest, the sea's bounty, and the simple gift of another day. The old stone church, weathered by centuries of storms, stands as a testament to this enduring devotion.

There is a saying passed down among the elders of the region: that God can be found not only within the walls of the chapel, but in the misty mornings that settle over Kilcloher's green hills. The land itself becomes a kind of prayer—each blade of grass, each rolling wave, a reminder of creation's quiet majesty.

Visitors who wander through Kilcloher often remark on the peace that lingers there. Perhaps it is the isolation, or the raw beauty of the coast. Or perhaps it is something the locals have always known: that in places like this, where the world feels untouched, the distance between the earthly and the divine grows wonderfully thin.

And so Kilcloher remains—a humble corner of the world where the land, the people, and God seem forever intertwined.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a narrative poem about a boy who dies by suicide jumping off a cliff into the sea in rural Ireland, and a compassionate figure named Argyle who defies the priest's refusal of a Christian burial.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Burial of Young Cormac

By the cliffs of grey Kilrannan where the wild Atlantic churns,
Where the gorse grows gold in springtime and the peat-smoke slowly turns,
There a boy named Cormac Doyle looked down upon the tide,
And the weight he could not carry pulled him to the ocean's side.

He was seventeen that April, with the sorrow no one saw,
For the young men do not speak of what breaks in them, and gnaws.
So he stood upon the headland where the fulmars wheeled and cried,
And he loosed his grief to heaven, and he stepped into the wide.

They recovered him by morning where the black rocks meet the foam,
And they carried him in silence to his weeping mother's home.
But when they came to Father Breen to lay the boy to rest,
He refused the consecrated ground, and crossed himself, and blessed—

"No suicide," the priest declared, "may lie in holy earth.
The Church has spoken clear on this since long before your birth.
He raised his hand against himself; he spurned the gift of life.
Beyond the wall he'll find his bed, past sanctuary and strife."

Then the mother fell to keening and the father turned away,
For who could fight the collar in that dark and bitter day?
The village bowed their heavy heads and murmured of the sin,
And the door of God's own garden would not let young Cormac in.

But an old man named Argyle stood leaning on the gate,
A stranger to their chapel, but no stranger to their fate.
He had wandered through the parish these long thirty years or more,
A mender of the fences, and a keeper of the poor.

"You would bury him in shadow, past the reach of every prayer,
As though the boy who suffered had no soul to carry there?
I have known the dark he walked in—I have felt that undertow.
It is not a door slammed shut on God. It is a place we go.

"You say he chose the falling. But you never saw him fight
The thousand secret mornings when he still chose to see light.
The illness in the spirit is no different from the flesh—
Would you damn a boy for fever? Would you scorn the drowning's thresh?"

But the priest would not be moved, and so the old man bowed his head,
And he took the boy himself, and to the mourning kin he said:
"Then I will make him holy ground, for God is not a wall.
He is the wideness of the sea that gathers up us all."

So Argyle dug the grave himself beneath a hawthorn tree,
On a green and gentle hillock overlooking Cormac's sea.
And he lined the earth with heather and with primrose, pale and sweet,
And he laid the boy with tenderness, a blanket round his feet.

Then he spoke no Latin over him, but words both plain and true:
"You were loved, and you are loved still, and there's nothing you must do
To earn a place in mercy, for it's given, never bought.
Rest now, gentle Cormac. You are more than what you fought."

And the mother came, and knelt with him, and father, sister, friend,
And they found in that small ceremony a grief that God could mend.
For the hawthorn is a holy tree in Ireland's ancient lore,
And it blossomed white that summer as it never had before.

Now the years have turned to decades, and old Argyle lies near,
In the same unblessed and blessed earth he made a garden here.
And the villagers still visit, and they've learned what love can teach:
That compassion is a sacrament no wall of stone can breach.

So remember young Cormac Doyle, and the man who would not turn,
Who saw the light in suffering that the righteous failed to learn.
For heaven is not measured by the rules that we defend,
But the tenderness we offer to the broken, in the end.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem in the style of Thomas Lynch featuring the recurring character Argyle, dealing with death, mercy, and the Catholic Church's treatment of suicide.
counterfactuals.output:
**Argyle and the Suicide**

They found the boy below the Cleggan road,
his neck at that unnatural cant, the rope
still arguing with gravity, the load
of him gone slack. The priest would not give hope

nor ground—no requiem, no bell, no plot
inside the wall where Christian bones were laid.
*Self-murder,* Fr. Kenny called the knot,
and turned his collar from the debt unpaid.

So Argyle came, as Argyle always came,
by hunger summoned, at the edge of things,
to where the mother, keening out her shame,
had set the bread upon the breast, the strings

of the poor corpse's shirt undone, a bowl
of ale beside the cold and swollen face.
He ate. He drank. He took into his soul
whatever sins the Church would not erase—

the last despair, the leap the boy called peace,
the fist he made against a silent God—
and swallowed them like communion, a release
no bishop signed, no chrism, no facade

of Latin over him. Just Argyle's throat
working the darkness down, the way a drain
takes in the flood, the way a leaking boat
still ferries someone over. In the rain

he wiped his mouth and would not meet their eyes.
*A man's a man,* he said, *and God's a door.
Whatever mercy is, it's not disguised
as men who keep the poor out of the poor.*

He knew the arithmetic of grace was wrong
that counted noose but never counted why—
the empty larder, or the winter long,
the small interior weathers where men die

before they die. He'd carried heavier freight:
old lechers, thieves, the ones who beat their wives,
all shriven by his belly at the gate.
Why should the boy who could not bear his life

be barred the field where lambs and liars slept?
So Argyle bore him, sin and rope and all,
inside himself, and something in him wept
that was not his, and climbed the churchyard wall

that night with a spade and a lantern's guttering flame
and dug a place the priest would not have blessed,
and laid the boy where no one knew his name
was written out of mercy, not confessed—

then ate his supper walking home, alone,
the ragged sacrament of what men fear:
that no one gets to heaven on his own,
and someone has to swallow what's left here.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a somber Irish elegy about drowning, funeral customs, and religious judgment, incorporating biblical allusions like the prodigal son and Christ's words on the cross.
counterfactuals.output:
# Lament for the Drowned

Beneath the grey Atlantic's ceaseless moan,
Where Sligo's currents drag the fishers down,
We keen for you, our lost and sea-swept own,
Whose bones now bed in salt, whose name will drown.

The women gathered at the cottage door,
Their shawls pulled black against the bitter dawn,
And laid you where the candle-flames adore
The pale, cold clay of one so young and gone.

The clay pipes rest upon the linen white,
The mirrors turned, the clocks all stopped and still,
While *caoineadh* rises through the mourning night—
That ancient grief no priest nor psalm can kill.

O prodigal, you left the father's fold
To chase the herring shoals through squall and spray,
And thought to come again with silver, gold,
But came home carried in the ebbing bay.

Would that the Father ran to meet you there,
With ring and robe and calf, the fatted feast—
Yet who can say what judgment waits, and where
The soul is weighed by God, and man, and priest?

They whisper that the sea has cursed your grave,
That unshriven you slipped beneath the foam;
The gossips count the sins they cannot save,
And bar your restless spirit from its home.

But hear the words that split the darkened sky,
When Christ Himself hung broken, spat-upon:
*"Why hast Thou now forsaken me?"*—the cry
Of every drowning soul when hope is gone.

And after: *"It is finished."* Let it be
Your absolution, though no bell was rung.
For He who wept was also lost at sea
Of human sorrow, dying, spurned, and young.

So we will lay the seaweed on your breast,
And light the rush-light 'gainst the coming morn,
And trust that God, who knows the storm-tossed rest,
Will gather even those the waves have torn.

Sleep now, where Owenmore meets ocean's swell,
No cross above, but Christ's own cross beneath—
For grace runs deeper than the parish bell,
And love outlasts the judgment, and the grief.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a free-verse poem set on the Irish coast where fishermen recover a young suicide's body, and a layman offers grace where the church withholds it.
counterfactuals.output:
The Grace of Salt Water

At dawn the boats came back heavier than they left,
their nets holding what no man wants to catch—
a boy, no more than nineteen,
his pockets weighted with the small stones
he must have gathered in the dark
like a child collecting something precious.

The sea gave him up gentle,
though he had asked it to keep him.

We knew his mother.
We knew the shape of his silence
in the back pew, the way he'd stopped
coming to the rail for bread and wine.
The priest would say the words
that fit a life like his into no consecrated ground—
outside the wall, they'd lay him,
past the reach of blessing,
where the nettles grow and no stone stands.

But old Tom Fahey, who'd never worn
a collar in his life, who smelled of tar
and forty years of hauling,
knelt down there on the shingle
and took the boy's cold hand in both of his.

*You're not lost,* he said,
loud enough for the gulls,
loud enough for the God
he wasn't sure believed in walls.
*Whatever brought you to the water,
whatever the dark said in your ear—
it lied. And if there's mercy anywhere,
it doesn't stop at a churchyard gate.*

He wept then, this hard man,
salt to salt,
and pressed his cracked lips to the boy's forehead
the way you'd kiss your own son goodnight.

The rest of us stood bareheaded in the wind.
No bell rang. No candle burned.
Only the sea kept its long confession
against the rocks,
and a fisherman's blessing
rose up over a body the world had failed—

as if grace were a thing
you could simply decide to give,
here, on the wet stones,
with your own two hands.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem exploring the tension between religious doctrine and human compassion, using the imagery of a "leap of faith" and reframing a suicide as a return to the father's embrace.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Ledge**

They told us it was sin, the final fall—
that grace withdraws its hand at that dark door,
that mercy has a limit after all,
a line the drowning are not pardoned for.

But I have knelt beside the emptied bed
and traced the shape of anguish in the sheet,
and I cannot believe the God who bled
would meet exhaustion with a colder heat.

You did not leap toward death. You leapt toward rest—
a body worn past what the flesh can bear,
a soul that fell not from but into a breast
already open, waiting for you there.

The doctrine draws its map of who is barred;
compassion asks what map could hold your pain.
If faith means anything, it trusts the Guard
of every gate keeps no one out in vain.

So let the theologians hold their court.
I only know the arms that made the deep
are wide enough to be a landing's port
for those the world could neither hold nor keep.

Not judgment at the bottom of the dark—
a Father running, as the story goes,
to meet the child while still a distant spark,
and fold him home, and ask no more than *those*.

---

*If you or someone you know is struggling, help is available. In the US, you can call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline). These themes are worth writing about—and worth reaching for support around, too.*
